AWS X-Ray sampling rules
Bedrock model invocation logging
cards.why: Transaction Search is the CloudWatch feature that indexes spans for the GenAI Observability views. Model invocation logging is separate and records prompts and completions, which is a privacy decision in its own right.

cards.prompt: Why should prompt and completion content capture be off by default in a law firm's agent telemetry?
options: It makes traces too slow to render
Prompts contain privileged client documents, so capturing them copies that text into the telemetry backend's retention and jurisdiction
OpenTelemetry does not support string attributes
LLM providers forbid logging their outputs
cards.why: A trace store is a second copy of client data with its own access controls, retention and possibly region. Record chunk ids, token counts and latencies by default; turn on content capture only for a scoped debugging window with approval.

cards.prompt: In newer OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, the attribute gen_ai.system was replaced by ___.
cards.why: The rename is one of several breaking changes while the conventions are in Development. Dashboards keyed on gen_ai.system silently go empty after an SDK upgrade.

cards.prompt: AgentCore Observability can only receive telemetry from agents that run on AgentCore Runtime.
cards.why: Agents on Runtime are auto-instrumented, but any agent instrumented with the ADOT SDK can send OTLP spans to CloudWatch's endpoint with SigV4, including ECS, on-premises or another cloud. Frameworks like Strands and LangChain already emit GenAI-convention spans.

explain.prompt: A client's Bedrock bill tripled last month and nobody changed the code. How do you find out why, and how do you stop it recurring?
explain.modelAnswer: First I go to the traces, because a bill is just the sum of gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and output_tokens across spans. I group spans by day and by operation to see whether the spike is more sessions, longer prompts, or more calls per session. Typical culprits: a tool-call loop where the agent retries the same failing tool dozens of times; a retrieval change that returns 50 chunks instead of 8 so every prompt is five times longer; a conversation history that is never trimmed; or a batch job someone pointed at production. The trace tree shows which: span count per session, prompt size per LLM span, and finish reasons. If I have no traces, that is finding number one. To prevent recurrence I emit cost per answer as a CloudWatch metric computed from token counts and model price, alert on spans per session and on daily spend per client, cap tool iterations in the agent loop, and put a hard budget in the agent framework. Then I add a cost assertion to the golden-set run so a prompt change that doubles tokens fails CI before it reaches the client.
rubric: Uses token attributes on spans to decompose the bill
Names concrete causes: loops, bigger prompts, untrimmed history
Diagnoses from span count and prompt size per session
Preventive metrics and alerts on cost and span count
Hard caps on iterations and a CI cost check

scenarios.situation: A Frankfurt-based law firm is deploying your agent on ECS in eu-central-1. The engineers want LangSmith for its debugging UI and have the default US endpoint and full prompt capture enabled in staging. The firm's DPO asks where client documents will be stored and under which jurisdiction.
scenarios.question: What do you set up for production?

options.text: Instrument with OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, keep message-content capture off, record chunk ids and token counts, and ship spans to CloudWatch in eu-central-1 (or LangSmith's EU endpoint) after the DPO signs off on retention.
options.why: The trace store is a second copy of client data; keeping content off and the backend in-region answers the DPO's question truthfully. OTel keeps you vendor-neutral so the debugging UI choice is reversible.

options.text: Skip tracing in production and rely on structured application logs with request ids, adding traces only when a problem is reported.
options.why: Logs with correlation ids do answer some questions and avoid the data-residency issue, but you lose token accounting per span and the tree view that finds loops. You will be reconstructing traces by hand during the first incident.

options.text: Keep the staging configuration: LangSmith US endpoint with full prompt and completion capture, because it makes debugging fastest.
options.why: Privileged German client documents would be copied into a US-hosted store with its own retention. That is a GDPR and professional-secrecy problem the firm cannot accept, however good the UI.

nodes.title: Guardrails and Approval Gates
nodes.tease: The model 'approved' a settlement letter and sent it. Nobody asked a human. Where was the gate?

lesson.body:
Guardrails are layers, and none of them is the retrieval filter. **Input validation**: schema and length checks, allow-listed tools, prompt-injection detection on anything that came from a document rather than the user. **Output validation**: request structured output against a JSON schema and validate it server-side, the way ASP.NET model binding plus FluentValidation treats a request body; never let free text drive a side effect. **Human approval gates**: any irreversible or expensive action (send to a client, file with a court, delete, spend above a threshold) pauses the workflow, persists state, and resumes only on an explicit approval, like a manual approval on an Azure DevOps environment. An agent that 'asks itself' for permission has no gate.

**Amazon Bedrock Guardrails** adds managed policies you attach to Converse/Invoke or call directly through `ApplyGuardrail`, which works with any model including self-hosted ones. Policies: content filters (Hate, Insults, Sexual, Violence, Misconduct, Prompt Attack, each with a strength), denied topics, word filters, sensitive information filters (PII entities or regex; block or mask), **contextual grounding checks**, and **Automated Reasoning checks** (GA 6 August 2025), which compile a written policy into formal logic and prove or refute statements instead of estimating a confidence. Grounding checks score grounding (is every claim supported by the source) and relevance (does it answer the query) against thresholds from 0 to 0.99; they run on the output only, and cap at 100,000 characters of source, 1,000 of query and 5,000 of response. With `ApplyGuardrail` you tag content blocks with `qualifiers`: `grounding_source` for the retrieved passages, `query`, and an unqualified or `guard_content` block for the answer. Billing is per policy per 1,000 text units of up to 1,000 characters each: content filters and denied topics $0.15, PII filters and grounding checks $0.10, Automated Reasoning $0.17 per policy; regex and word filters are free.

What guardrails do not do: decide who may see a document. A denied topic is not an ethical wall; that remains the retrieval-time permission filter.
lesson.snippet:
resp = bedrock_runtime.apply_guardrail(
    guardrailIdentifier=GUARDRAIL_ID, guardrailVersion="3",
    source="OUTPUT",                      # grounding checks only run on output
    content=[
        {"text": {"text": "\n\n".join(c.text for c in retrieved_chunks),
                  "qualifiers": ["grounding_source"]}},     # <= 100,000 chars
        {"text": {"text": question, "qualifiers": ["query"]}},  # <= 1,000 chars
        {"text": {"text": draft_answer}},                      # content to guard, <= 5,000
    ],
)
if resp["action"] == "GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED":
    # inspect resp["assessments"][0]["contextualGroundingPolicy"]["filters"]
    # each filter has type GROUNDING | RELEVANCE, score, threshold, action
    return abstain("I could not ground an answer in the retrieved documents.")

# irreversible step: stop and wait for a human, do not let the model decide
if action.kind in {"send_to_client", "file_with_court"}:
    checkpoint.save(state)
    approvals.request(action, approver=supervising_partner)
    raise PausedForApproval(action.id)

source.title: Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses - Amazon Bedrock

cards.prompt: What range of threshold values does a Bedrock contextual grounding check accept for grounding and relevance?
options: 0 to 1 inclusive
cards.why: A threshold of 1 is rejected because it would block every response; 0.99 is the maximum. Responses whose grounding or relevance score falls below the threshold are treated as hallucinations and blocked or flagged.

cards.prompt: Bedrock's contextual grounding check evaluates the input prompt as well as the model's output.
cards.why: Grounding needs a response to compare against the source, so it only runs on output. Content filters, denied topics, word filters and PII filters are the policies that run on both input and output.

cards.prompt: Bedrock's ___ API lets you run a guardrail against any model's text, including self-hosted or third-party models that never touch Bedrock inference.
cards.why: ApplyGuardrail decouples the policy from the model, so one guardrail can govern a Bedrock model, an on-prem model and a vendor API consistently. It also means you can run grounding checks on a draft before any side effect.

cards.prompt: In an ApplyGuardrail call for a RAG answer, which qualifier marks the retrieved passages?
options: guard_content
query
grounding_source
context
cards.why: grounding_source is the reference the answer is checked against, query is the user's question, and the unqualified or guard_content block is the text being guarded. Content tagged grounding_source or query is excluded from the other policies unless you also add guard_content.

cards.prompt: What is the correct implementation of a human approval gate before an agent sends a letter to a client?
options: Add 'always ask the user before sending' to the system prompt
Have the model call an approve_self tool that returns true when it is confident
Persist the workflow state, stop execution, notify an approver, and resume only when an authenticated human approves
Send the letter and allow recall within 60 seconds
cards.why: A gate must be enforced by the orchestrator, not requested of the model. Checkpointing and resuming on approval is the same pattern as a manual approval stage on an Azure DevOps environment; a prompt instruction is optional by construction.

cards.prompt: A denied-topics policy in Bedrock Guardrails is an acceptable substitute for retrieval-time permission filters between matters.
cards.why: Topic filters classify what the text is about, not who may see it; two matters can share every topic. Access control has to happen before retrieval returns a chunk, and guardrails run after the text already exists.

cards.prompt: How do Automated Reasoning checks differ from contextual grounding checks?
options: They are the same feature under a new name
Automated Reasoning compiles a written policy into formal logic and proves or refutes statements; grounding uses an ML model to score confidence against a source
Automated Reasoning runs on input; grounding runs on output
Automated Reasoning only works with Amazon's own models
cards.why: Automated Reasoning (GA August 2025) encodes rules such as eligibility or approval policies as logic and returns findings like valid or invalid with explanations; grounding is a probabilistic check on whether claims are supported by retrieved text. They catch different errors and can be combined.

cards.prompt: The grounding source for a Bedrock contextual grounding check is limited to ___ characters.
cards.why: Source is capped at 100,000 characters, the query at 1,000 and the response at 5,000. For a 50-chunk prompt you will hit the source cap, which is another reason to rerank down to a handful of chunks before generation.

explain.prompt: Describe the guardrail layers you would put around an agent that drafts and sends client-facing letters.
explain.modelAnswer: I think in layers from the outside in. Input: the request is validated against a schema, the agent only has the tools this workflow needs, and anything retrieved from documents is treated as untrusted text and scanned for prompt injection before it reaches the model. Retrieval: the permission filter decides which documents it may draw from; no guardrail replaces that. Generation: the draft is produced as structured output against a JSON schema, recipient, matter id, body, cited chunk ids, and validated server-side like any API request body. Then a Bedrock contextual grounding check runs on the body with the retrieved chunks as grounding_source, PII filters mask anything that should not leave the firm, and I verify every cited id exists. The critical layer is the approval gate: 'send' is an irreversible action, so the orchestrator checkpoints the state, stops, and notifies the supervising lawyer; it resumes only on their authenticated approval, never on the model's say-so. Every step is traced with token counts and chunk ids for audit. The model drafts; humans and deterministic code decide.
rubric: Input validation and injection scanning of retrieved text
Structured output validated server-side
Grounding check and PII masking before the side effect
Orchestrator-enforced human approval with persisted state
Permission filter at retrieval is separate from guardrails
Audit trace of the whole run

scenarios.situation: An agent drafts privilege-log entries for a Fortune 100 client's document production: for each withheld document it writes the date, author, recipients, privilege basis and a description, then a tool uploads the log to the production platform. The deadline is Friday. A reviewer notices one entry described a document as 'draft board minutes' when it was an email, and the privilege basis was invented.
scenarios.question: What do you change before resuming?

options.text: Produce each entry as structured output validated against a schema, run a contextual grounding check of description and basis against the document's own text, route any entry below threshold to a reviewer, and gate the upload tool behind an explicit human approval of the batch.
options.why: An invented privilege basis can waive privilege or draw sanctions, so the side effect must sit behind deterministic checks and a human. Grounding and schema validation catch the fabrication; the approval gate makes the upload an attorney's act, not the model's.

options.text: Have a second model call review each entry and correct it before upload, keeping the upload automatic to hit Friday.
options.why: A reviewer model reduces errors and is cheap, but it is another probabilistic step with no accountability, and the upload remains unsupervised. It is a reasonable addition inside the gate, not a replacement for it.

options.text: Lower the model temperature, add 'never invent a privilege basis' to the prompt, and resume automated uploads.
options.why: Prompt instructions are suggestions, not controls, and temperature does not prevent fabrication. You would be producing a court-facing document with the same failure mode and no way to catch it.

questions.prompt: Design a system that lets lawyers ask questions over 2 million documents across hundreds of matters. Walk me through ingestion, indexing, retrieval, security, answer generation and how you would know it works.
questions.modelOutline: Start with constraints: per-matter confidentiality, ethical walls, citations that must be verifiable, EU data residency, and a budget. Ingestion: S3 landing, event-driven workers (Step Functions or Kafka consumers) that parse and OCR, dedupe by hash, extract metadata (matter, custodian, date, privilege) into sidecars, idempotent on doc id. Chunking: structure-aware, Article/Section boundaries with heading breadcrumbs and parent/child, email threads by message. Index: OpenSearch or Elasticsearch, hybrid BM25 plus kNN with quantized vectors, partitioned per matter or client, RRF fusion. Security: entitlements resolved server-side and applied as a pre-filter in every query, deny by default. Reranker over the top 50, keep eight. Generation with chunk ids, citations verified against retrieved ids, abstain when nothing grounds. Audit log of user, filter, chunk ids, tokens, model. Guardrails: grounding check, PII masking, approval gates for any action. Evaluation: golden set per matter type, recall@k and faithfulness in CI, cost per answer tracked in traces. Close with the rollout: pilot one matter, measure, expand.
rubric: Ingestion pipeline: parse/OCR, dedupe, metadata extraction, idempotent and event-driven
Structure-aware chunking with breadcrumbs and parent/child for legal documents
Per-matter (or per-client) hybrid index: BM25 plus kNN fused with RRF, quantized vectors
Permission filters derived server-side and applied as pre-filters, deny by default
Cross-encoder reranker over a shortlist before generation
Citations tied to chunk ids and verified; abstains when ungrounded
Audit log of user, filter, chunk ids, model and tokens per request
Golden evaluation set with retrieval and faithfulness metrics run in CI

questions.prompt: How do you know the agent's answers are good?
questions.modelOutline: Define 'good' as three measurable things: the right evidence was retrieved, the answer is faithful to that evidence and actually answers the question, and the system abstains when it should. Build a golden set with domain experts: 100-200 questions with labelled relevant chunks and reference answers, stratified by type including unanswerable. Measure retrieval with recall@k and nDCG, deterministic and free; measure generation with RAGAS-style faithfulness (supported claims over total), response relevancy, context recall. Use an LLM judge from a different family with pointwise rubrics, swapped orderings for comparisons, and calibrate it against lawyer grades before trusting it. Run the set in CI on every prompt, model or index change and gate deploys on regressions. In production, sample traces for judged faithfulness, track thumbs-down and corrected answers, feed them back into the set, and watch cost and latency per answer alongside quality.
rubric: Separates retrieval quality from generation quality
Golden set built with domain experts, stratified, includes unanswerable questions
Retrieval metrics (recall@k, nDCG) that need no LLM
Generation metrics: faithfulness, response relevancy, context recall
LLM-as-judge biases named and mitigated, calibrated against humans
Evaluation runs in CI and gates deploys
Production monitoring: sampled judging, user feedback loop, cost per answer
